projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward Frank DeFoe was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Edward Frank Defoe. Mr. Defoe served in the U.S. Army with the 103rd Division, 409th Regiment, Company B. Ed's highest rank was PFC and he served in the European Theater. I'm Tom Swope and this telephone interview was recorded on April 25, 2003. Ed was 84 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, I was living on Charles. We had -- we had just gotten married and we lived upstairs with some people --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: -- that we didn't know, you know. And just a couple of rooms cuz I new I was going in so--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Twenty-one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Twenty-one. Were you working then?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well share as much as you can about that?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well my wife and I were sitting around listening to the radio, cuz television wasn't invented, you know, and all of a sudden we got it on the radio. And she says, Ed, Ed, Carl is down there, that's my buddy and she was ma's buddy too -- also we were real connected with the family. And so we waited for a call from her, and yep, that was true, that's what was going on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your personal reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Like oh, oh. I'll be going quicker than I even thought.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum. So had you already been contacted about being inducted into the Army at that point?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the Army?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '44. So were you a -- you were working that time up till 1944 then?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Uh-huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have a job deferment or just hadn't been called?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I just hadn't been called.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your were lucky for a few years anyway?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when in 1944, early in 1944?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: During the summer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I don't remember exactly when, I suppose its on my discharge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, it's -- I don't know. It must have been around June or July, right in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now before you went into the service, do you remember doing anything for the war efforts as far as scrap drives or whatever?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No. I was just a kid, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was rationing much of a problem for you?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Not at all. It was only two of us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. So you were able to get enough of what you wanted?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I made $17 a week? I thought I was doing all right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And you had enough tires and that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that a difficult thing to get? Decent tires for the car?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Very much. Very much. Cuz I had procured a Packard convertible with 30,000 miles on it. It was a 1932. It was a beauty. Never been in an accident, and I don't think it was hardly out of a garage, and I tried to get tires for it, and, there was no way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: A guy I was working with, he said my brother works for -- I don't no some tire outfit in Chicago -- and I will see if I can do something there. And he couldn't, so I sold it after a while to him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: He must have had tires some place.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well. So what can --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That was about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well that was down in Camp Fannon with Ed Easter, do you know Ed Easter?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No, I don't?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, he's in Company B, a Sargent.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And we headed down Camp Fannon in Texas.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Nice and warm and that sort of thing. And in 17 weeks, we were gone.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything unusual or interesting happen during your training?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Not at all. No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Pretty routine?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Routine?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Routine, yeah, yeah, routine I think, ah this service ain't so bad. Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what, 17 weeks of training, and then you shipped overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, I think it was a week at home here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum. So what can you tell me about the trip overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well it was a lot of water. We went on a boat you know, they didn't fly anybody I don't guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: On the Wakefield, USS Wakefield. It was a troop thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And everybody -- lots of people got sick but I didn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your secret, how did you avoid that?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I don't know. Just luck I guess. But there were no storms or anything we got there in, I think, about a week.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um, hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: About a week, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was that a pretty big convoy?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I don't know I have no idea, probably, what maybe, two thousand people.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So it only took you a week to make the crossing?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, about a week.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Pretty good time then. Must have been a fast ship?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I don't know. Wasn't fast enough.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then you landed in England?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you land in England or France?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No, in England.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: England, and then we got off and got into a troop train a "forty and eight", do you know what a "forty and eight" is?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And we went to - right across the bay from La Havre, France.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So the other side --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Sof Haven(ph) I think, or Salt Haven(ph), Sant Haven(ph), or something, and then we got on a boat there and went to La Havre.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you weren't in England very long at all?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Not at all, not at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um, hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Just enough to see a couple of those bombs that the Krauts were shooting at them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So a couple of buzz bombs came over?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: There you go. That's what you call them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything come close?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Not that I know of no. Not in England. No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: They were bombed out in the country someplace. But there was couple of boats, ships I mean, that were sunk in the harbor when we got there. Kind of, your saying to yourself, whoa, man, I'm glad I made it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So then you landed in La Havre, this is probably what, maybe the fall of '44?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Somewhere around there?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Cold.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Cold there. And we got assigned to our company and then we were all divided up and different guys, everybody you know, depending on your name whether it began with a or z.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And that's how I got into the 103rd.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So at that point, in La Havre, you were assigned to the 103rd?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No. We had to know go to Ipinole(ph)?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Epenole(ph), okay.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That was one of those camps where they--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you went to a replacement camp first then. Is that--

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And that was it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When did you join up with the 103rd then? Do you remember, approximately, I don't need a date.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: A couple of days.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, within a couple of days after that. So you were with the 103rd probably, well probably -- -

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Right after they got captured.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, right after Selastad(ph)?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: We were replacements for those guys.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Ah.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That fast.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. So you replaced my dad?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: There you go.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So this would probably be sometime like December of '44. I think they were captured on December 1st or 2nd, is when all those guys were captured?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh, is that right? I didn't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, well that's what is says in the regimental history anyway. So for the purposes of the tape you were 409th Regiment, Company B. Right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Of the 103rd?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yep. Didn't mean nothing to me, but you know, it sure did afterwards, now that your with your guy --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: -- the guys that you're going to be with.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. What was is like for you being thrown into the Army, thinking back probably on your training, being thrown in with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Fine. It was neat. Yeah, it was neat. Find out all about the weather, you know, because I didn't travel much in those days. And it was nice -- I got in all with Southern guys -- we used to -- really kid around, kid me about everybody in Minnesota having web feet, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Because we have so many lakes here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That sort of thing. It was -- it was great.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I guess ___ but great.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Did you make some close buddies early on when you joined Company B?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, sure did. Did -- oh yeah, probably the next few days. Another replacement came in and he asked me, he says are you Defoe, and I said yeah. Well, he says my name is Bowls, big Southern guy. Little Southern guy and he looked up at me like a pet dog he -- I just liked him right away. And he says, you and I are on guard tonight. He says, now I gotta tell you something right now, I'm a follower not a leader, and don't forget it. I said we're going to have a heck of a time because, so am I. So we got to be real buddies. He was getting so -- he well, he was kind of deaf.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And so we did a lot of talking with sign language, not the real sign language, but enough to know what the other guy was doing you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Making fools of ourselves, but it was worth it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So, yes, Billy and I hung together real, real close. He was a nice guy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah. I thought to myself, this ain't the fun I thought it was going to be. Get to travel, but, jeez. But that was about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where was that?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: It was just out there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Somewhere in Europe?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Somewhere there, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what else were you thinking?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: ___ knew that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What else were you thinking when your were there?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I want to go home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. So we're talking about your first day of combat there, so did that go okay for the Company?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh yeah, oh yeah. I do know that when they were taking us up towards the front line there was a guy, a soldier, Kraut soldier in the road, and he obviously was shot dead.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And I couldn't make myself believe that this wasn't a dummy of some kind, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: What are they trying to do to us. But it wasn't, it was wartime.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Then I kind of woke up, you know, now we're at it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So what did you guys do to pass the time when you weren't in the middle of combat?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Just "BS".

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: "BS"?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, we was in combat most of the time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: We had, I think, more time in our outfit than a good share of them had, front line stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So we did just what we could do, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now at that point, the 103rd was probably in the Southern flank of the Battle of the Bulge; right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Chances are, yeah --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So your were directly involved in the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, that's what that cardboard thing says. But I asked them when I left down in, in -- Forest, pardon my -- fort, the one in Wisconsin anyway.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: When we got discharged, and I asked about it, and I says I think we were in the Bulge. I think we should have another star and he says "You want to stay in this 'bleep' army or do you want to go home?" Oh well, forget it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. I mean you were -- if you weren't directly involved you were certainly just a few miles away from where it was happening?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No, we were involved.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were involved. That's what my dad always told me too?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh, is that right?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you're right, you look at the list of units involved in the Battle of the Bulge, and the 103rd is not listed there? So they --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I got a thing here that says we were.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right then.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I'm looking at it now. The history of World War II. It's the size of one of those posters you buy, you know, with rock singers and stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Big like that and its got the thing -- history of the whole and entire war from 1939 up until 1945.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And there we are, with our patch.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As being involved in the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, there you go?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: With our patch. With a --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: With a cactus, right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And there's only one -- two -- two I think. There's two others besides -- two other patches that's showing here.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So it's kind of neat.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's very good. This is a poster?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I don't know who made it, but whoever did -- but probably one of our guys, who knows.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- that made it. Well I'm going to go back and check my official West Point history and see if they got it right. But, yeah, you look at other things and they claim that the 103rd wasn't directly involved in it, so --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Just for kicks, see if you find anything on the "R Deans Forest."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I will look for that?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That one too. Some of the guys say we were, one tree looks just like another.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right. So what else can you tell me? What else memorable happened for you during that time?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, we did what we had to do. Easter got hit -- I don't know if Easter got hit -- but our Lieutenant Mulholland, he got hit and a few of the other guys, Clayton got hit.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And that was -- you can't tell where the bullets are coming from, so I just-- just as soon as the bullets started flying I duck behind a tree, but I didn't know who to shoot at because you couldn't see anybody and, so I escaped that one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, so did you lose any close buddies?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, I suppose. Some of the guys, yeah, but I don't remember their names anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: There were so many of us, you know?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. What was your specific job with the Company?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Infantry.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Infantry. Were you just -- basically a rifleman? You were not --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That's all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I didn't even know I was a Corporal until I got out and looked at my discharge papers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They didn't give you that information while your were still over there?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Not at all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well that's interesting. So you just saw that your were discharged as a Corporal?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Uh huh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you give them more money when your were over there?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I don't know, I had it all sent home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. So your backpay, or whatever, somebody else spent it for you.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No use having money. There were no stores.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Do you remember mail call? Getting letters or packages from home?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Um hum, but I didn't get -- there's packages, you know my wife used -- we were, like I say, first married and she wasn't much of cook. Well, I won't say she wasn't much of a cook, but at least she knew how to make chocolate chip cookies. So she was sending me chocolate chip cookies, which I was trading off for --I don't remember what -- souvenirs or something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: There were so many of them, but lot of them -- a lot of that I didn't get. They got short-stopped at the Army post office or something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was there a lot of souvenir collecting going on?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No. We was infantry man, we didn't have nothing to carry it with.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: You put it in your pocket.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And you're walking for a thousand miles. You don't want any extra weight to begin with.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: But, yeah, there were places that we made into that we -- like typewriters and all them sort of good things like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. So what came next for the Company after the Bulge early in '45?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well we were still -- they were still active.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I went -- came home, I was transferred. Frye, you know Fry? Maybe you don't know him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I know the name, but no I don't think -- I might have met him?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Transferred to the Ninth division -- this was an African outfit. They had been fighting in Africa.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Depending on points and then I was transferred from there to the 71st and from the 71st -- this was after the war -- and from the 71st to a -- what do you call those units that build things?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Combat engineers or --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Engineer outfit, I don't remember the number -- 2038 or something like that, and got on a boat and the rest is history.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you come back?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '45. So you weren't actually part of the occupation forces then?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just doing your time over there until you could come back?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Until you had enough points, right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, yeah but, yeah I was there six months afterward. Maybe it was six weeks, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you on VE day?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That's Europe?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I was on guard duty, and ah, I remembered it so well because, I was on guard duty a whole lot. And, I see a Jeep coming down the road and then I'm wondering, you know, what's cooking here. And they look like GIs. So, they stopped and I got aboard, and they took me back to the Company and said the war was over with and I said sure it is, and it was. And so there your are.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particular celebrations on that day?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: You know, oh yeah we got to see a movie. I don't remember what it was, probably "Dear John" or something.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: But that was about it. Nothing exciting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, at that point, did you think perhaps your were headed for the Pacific?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Not at that point, well yeah, at that point, because they were listing guys in the lunch room. We had a regular what we called a lunchroom instead of a shack, or nothing, and they posted it in there, and so everybody was looking at that as they go in and out. They had a Defreeze(ph) there, and they had a Defeel(ph) and all that kind of thing, but no Defoe. By that time, then they finished it off in Japan, and that's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were still in Europe when Japan was bombed I assume?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now what did the guys -- how did the guys react to that?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I don't have to sweat it out going overseas, I mean going over there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any comprehension of what an atomic bomb was?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Uh uh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Just knew it was --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Just a "big mother."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A "big mother"?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was your reunion with your wife like when you finally got back?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh, well -- oh it was at the depot down here in St. Paul. And my folks and her mom, I guess, couple of other people were -- met me at the train and that's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum. Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after the war?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: You know, my son-in-law said the exact same thing about three weeks ago.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And he wrote me a letter - he lives six-blocks away - he wrote me a letter asking me, I don't know if he thought it was something real personal or what, and he asked me what -- how did I handle it when I come home. And I said, well, I was down in the driveway wiping off my Packard and she came downstairs with envelopes in her hand, and they were bills, and I thought, well, guess I got to go to work, and I had the job waiting for me, so that's what I did?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum. So that was it, just get on with your life?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Exactly right. I tried to get in, I didn't really try, but Waldorf Paper Company was a big company and I kept thinking to myself, you know, I got so tired of driving and driving and driving out here, you know, with the snow and putting on chains on my truck, I want an inside job. So I went over there to Waldorf and they hired me. And then I had to go over to Northwest Hospital and get okayed there. And then I came back, and he was going to take me to my job, and as we going up those steel steps, I started to get kind of squeamish, because it was kind of thick with smell--

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And I mean smell of iron or -- smell, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And so we were walking along, and I happened to look on the side and there was a sign that said exit, and so I made a quick right turn and went down the fire escape back to my car and then went back to my old job.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: I wonder what that guy thought.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You just didn't want to make that change, huh?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Yeah. No, it was too confined, I guess. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you first got back there, did you talk much about the war or think about it much?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Not unless you met somebody that was with you, but I hadn't -- we didn't talk about it all actually, until Art Clayton called and -- called me in '91 and asked me if I wanted to go to a reunion. And I says I can't because that's -- was when my wife was sick.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So I didn't go, and he sent me some -- he sent me some pictures and stuff of the guys and I recognize some of them and, oh man, I wanted to go so bad, but I didn't know how in the heck I could cuz Ma was in real bad shape then too, and she was in bad shape for many years.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And so I got the few guys that Art gave me the addresses of and wrote letters about it and, then he -- at the next one, the next one that came, the next reunion of following year in '92, and it's strange. I was out there on the front porch, we got a front porch with windows and stuff on it, and a gal came along and rapped on the door. So I answered the door. She told me she was from Health East -- no, she told me she was from Wilder, and well my ears kind of perked up, because Wilder was only like ten minutes away from here and so I told her about -- oh, and then she just, just completely says, "You know what Mr. Defoe, if you ever wanted to go some place," she says they have a place that you can leave your wife for x-number of days, and oh man, then the whole thing came tumbling, you know, wow, maybe I'll have a chance to go on to these reunions. So then she says -- I told her the date and everything and she came up here, upstairs up here to my little office -- skinny office here and use my phone. She came down says, "You know what? You're all set." Wow, I was so happy. Cost me -- five days it cost me near 900 bucks but man I would have given them $1800. I was so anxious and glad. I got done there to -- it was down in Texas -- Anaheim that's where it was -- down in Anaheim, and I looked at one guy. Didn't know anybody, and then one guy had his back to me and he said "You know he says, Defoe's coming and he looks like, oh, oh" he turned around and said, there he is." And so we got to meet some of the other guys and, oh, it was just great. Most of our outfit, our squad was still intact, more or less. We've lost some since then, only 12 men to a squad, so there's probably half of them left. Fought partial buddies __

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So it was real good and I haven't missed since. I took her down the first few years to Wilder and they took care of her there while I was gone. And then the last 10 years, of course, she was in the nursing home permanently, so I had no problem.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now was Art your foxhole buddy?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: 0h yeah. Art was, Clayton.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you guys talk about in the foxhole?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Talk about home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Your job and your home, that's all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did the two of you have any interesting experiences over there?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Did I?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That you and Art --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh, we was on guard duty a few times.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No, nothing exciting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No adventures or misadventures?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, you got that notice, the one with the cabbages?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, go ahead and put that on tape too so I have it on this tape?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh, well, one of the guys, I can't remember the names anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's okay?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: -- from Massachusetts there were three or four of us in a house and we were on guard duty, of course, and this guy come along, and I mean he was off, and then it was my turn to go up and replace him. We were looking out the window, kind of an attic-like, and he says, "Before I go, take a look down there." So I looked down there. "You see any of those things moving?" I looked and I looked. Yeah, it looked like that one moved. Oh, what do you think? Yeah. So then I come downstairs. And so Clayton and I, brave soldiers you know, says we'll go out and take a look. So we open the door real carefully. Got on our bellies, and there was kind of hump in front of the door, so he made over to the left, he made on that side of the hump and I made on that side of the hump, and, on my side of the hump there was an outside toilet and I heard noises inside the toilet, and I thought, oh man, and so I moseyed up to the toilet and put my gun barrel in the door, and I was going to fire it, but then I thought I better not. I don't want to make any noise, and then I got brave and looked around the other side, and sure enough, it was a crow crawling around the toilet seat which the toilet seat had snow on it. So then we looked over and then we found out they were cabbage heads. It didn't really move, but you look at something long enough and you swear it moves.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh huh?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh yeah, so the rear echelon got charge of that cuz somebody took off and reported it, you know. I know it made the -- what do you call the paper there?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh --

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: "Stars and Stripes."

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: "Stars and Stripes?" That you were attacked by cabbage heads?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Uh huh. Exactly. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But nobody tried to pick off any of the cabbage heads?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you eat them?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: No. Just glad enough to find them. We weren't in reserve at that time, we were to go in, but some of the guys got shot up pretty good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So that was -- that was it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. When you think about your experiences over there does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Oh no, whole lot of them like the cabbage one and then riding the horses with Billy and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that again so we can get that on tape?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Well, Billy come from a farm down in Texas. That was my itty, bitty buddy, Billy Bowls, and he come from a four-thousand acre farm down there, and so he knew horses backwards and forwards and he kept saying there was in the field, like there was horses roaming around he said, "you know" he says, "my legs are killing me." And so we kind of decided maybe we should get a horse, and so we broke ranks and away we went. So we got a horse. Well he climbed on one of them just like it was your Volkswagon, and of course, I couldn't, because that horse was so tall and big and ain't no saddle on these things. So I crawled up on an overturn truck and he led the horse -- they had bridles, but they didn't have any --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: -- any saddles. So he took me over by the truck and I climbed on. So then we started to wonder where our outfit was. This is not GI stuff, you know what I'm saying, not protocol.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So his horse and my horse must have been buddies, because every time his horse trotted mine did too, and then I was losing my seat because I was getting over to one side, and nothing to grab onto, and I didn't want to hurt the horse and pull the mane because I was afraid he'd get mad.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So after a little bit then I -- his horse went through something I don't know what it was and then my horse got kind of panicky. I went off landing on my back. I busted the butt of my rifle, lost my helmet. So I got up and I was cussing that deal and here come Billy riding up and he's laughing so hard he almost fell off himself, he was laughing so hard. Then we took off with our horses for a while and then we met a Red Cross truck and they stopped and asked us -- it was just the two of us, oh and before that, we was going over toward a knoll sort of like a cliff and a shot rang out and the dust kind of went up in the field, up so somebody was shooting at us. So we went through that sign language I said before.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So Billy went over on the right side. I was going to go on the left-hand side and all of sudden I heard a bang and then I looked around and here comes Billy, little bow legs, and his gun hanging on his side, just a picture. So he gave me that sign you know, when you make that "o" with your fingers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And so then went along and went down with the Red Cross truck and then we got off early before we got into town, because we didn't want anybody to know what we had done, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: So we hiked into town and nobody even missed us. Poor Billy, his legs always hurt him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. He made it -- he survived the war though, right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He survived the war right?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: He survived the war. He had a time afterward with his kid going someplace I don't know, but, yeah, I seen him back in 1989.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And decided to get together and we did. And that was when Ma was still sick, but then we made it and went down to see him. It was really -- he had a -- we found the house and everything and a gal -- I got out. We took an RV down, but I rapped on the door and the door opened up, and the most -- there was the most luscious looking gal I had ever seen come answering the door. And I thought, uh oh, I'm in the wrong house. I says, "Do you know where Billy Bowls lives?" And she says, "Yeah, right here, come on in." Oh man, so then I talked to Billy a little bit and went out and got Ma and her friend that had come along with us, and we got together and as we -- we stayed there for about a week, and then Billy and I -- we hugged as we were leaving, and he says "You know, it's the first time I ever hugged a guy" and I said, "yeah, me too." So he started to cry and then he went back to the house and we went in the van and away we went.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: And then I got -- he came to the reunions for, oh three or four times. His son would put him on the -- a train and I mean -- on an airplane. And I'd collect him when we got to wherever where we were for the reunion and we worked that out for a while till the last year. The last year I say he couldn't make it and then he died the next year. He wasn't there anymore.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Um hum?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: But we were real, real good buddies.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah? Any other vivid memories of that time.

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: Ah, no I can't think of any.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Edward Frank DeFoe
sp.p: That covers it pretty good.
